notes:
I've written notes below for most verses. Two parts of your brief came back thin. I found no teachers from specific denominations (Lutheran, Methodist, Baptist and so on) commenting on this chapter. I also found no Catholic, Orthodox or prosperity / word of faith / hyper-grace readings of it. The only Catholic material was a list of Douay-Rheims cross-references, with no commentary. Where the sources I did read disagree with each other, I've noted it. I ran out of fetches before reading Gill, the Pulpit Commentary or the NET notes in full, so only what showed up in search snippets from those is included.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Guzik says this is a *command* to love. Love isn't left to feelings; people choose whether to love the LORD. God commanded Israel to love Him. Love is not a matter left entirely up to the impulses or feelings of God's people. People choose to love the LORD or to not love Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/
- He links love and obedience through John 14:15. Real love for Jesus will be seen in obedience. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/
- Ellicott: "keep his charge" literally means keep his keeping, i.e., all that is to be kept in obedience to Him, and "always" is literally "all the days." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says "charge" is what he has appointed to be observed and done (cf. Leviticus 8:35; Numbers 1:53); more fully explained by his statutes, and his judgments, and his commandments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/11-1.htm
- A homily in the Pulpit Commentary grounds obedience in gratitude. It warns that people who make good works the root of salvation instead of the fruit of salvation, are reversing the whole procedure of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-11.html

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: anyone under twenty at the Exodus would still be alive, so this speech would hit home with every man of about forty-five. "Discipline" may mean God's punishment of the Egyptians in anger, or of Israel in love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm
- The Treasury of Scripture Knowledge (TSK), quoted on Precept Austin, thinks Moses was speaking especially to the elders. They saw these events in their youth and were bound to tell the next generation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62493/

**vv. 3–5**
- Guzik: Moses wants Israel to think about what *God* has done, not what people have done. The works of God were more important to think about than the works of men. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/

**v. 4**
- On "to this day," Guzik quotes Merrill. The pharaohs after the Exodus (Thutmose IV and Amenhotep III) couldn't field large armies until after about 1400 B.C. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/

**v. 6**
- Guzik says Dathan and Abiram were Korah's main partners in his rebellion (Numbers 16), and perhaps the ones who started it. God took Moses' side. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/
- Ellicott uses this verse to argue that Deuteronomy's author knew about the priesthood conflict in Korah's rebellion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: literally, "your eyes are the witnesses (the seers)." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm
- Guzik, quoting Merrill: having seen so much made Israel highly accountable. "They could not plead either ignorance or lack of personal accountability." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: "commandments" is literally singular. It is one course of action rather than many details which is enjoined. "Possess" means finishing the conquest in detail. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm

**v. 9**
- The Pulpit Commentary says "prolong your days" refers rather to Israel's continuance as a nation, than to the long life of the individual. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-11.html
- Utley agrees: This is not an individual promise of longevity but a cultural promise of stability to a society which honors the Law of God https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-11

**v. 10**
- Guzik says "irrigated on foot" refers to foot-powered pumps lifting Nile water onto the fields. He quotes Merrill on a paddle-wheel device run by pedals. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/
- Ellicott thinks it means either carrying water or opening small channels with the foot. He also cites Rashi: Egypt, even Goshen, was not as good as Israel's land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm

**v. 11**
- Ellicott passes on a Jewish saying: God waters the land while you sleep. He compares it to the parable in Mark 4:26–27. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm
- Guzik: depending on rain was meant to keep Israel depending on God, and that dependence is a gift, not a burden. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: "cares for" is literally "seeks." He finds it hard not to think of heaven here, and of Jesus' words, "I go to prepare a place for you." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm
- Guzik says God's special care for the land holds both then and now. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Deu/Deu-11.cfm
- Matthew Henry: the land would be fruitful because of God's blessing more than its soil, as long as Israel stayed close to God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_011.cfm
- Spurgeon preached a New Year sermon on vv. 10–12, "Canaan on earth." https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62493/

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: here the formal promises of reward and threats of punishment begin, as in Leviticus 26, Deuteronomy 28 and the end of the Sermon on the Mount. He cites Rashi: don't serve God to get rich or famous; do everything out of love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm
- Guzik ties the condition to Matthew 6:33. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/
- Utley: the Hebrew doubles the word "obey" for emphasis. It means "to hear so as to do!" https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-11

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: the early rain came after sowing and the late rain just before harvest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm
- Guzik: the promise matters because Baal, the Canaanite god of weather and rain, would tempt Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/
- Gill, citing the Targum, puts the early rain around October and the late rain around March. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/11-14.htm
- Matthew Henry also reads the rain as a picture of spiritual comforts (Hosea). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_011.cfm

**v. 15**
- Ellicott, following Rashi: being satisfied is a blessing of its own. It is possible to eat and not be satisfied. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm

**vv. 16–17**
- Ellicott reads "be careful" as "when you are satisfied," comparing Deuteronomy 8:10–11. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm
- Guzik: prosperity can fool people into thinking they earned their blessings. He points to the drought under Ahab (1 Kings 17:1) as this very judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/
- *What the Bible Teaches*, quoted on Precept Austin, says the principle still applies today, partly as a spiritual famine. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62493/

**v. 18**
- Ellicott: these commands repeat Deuteronomy 6:6–9. Jewish readers said Israel would remember them in exile, if not before. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm
- Guzik treats the hand and forehead signs as symbols (from Exodus 13:9, 16) for keeping truth always in view. He notes the later Jewish custom of wearing scripture boxes (phylacteries). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/
- The Pulpit Commentary: the sign on the hand reminds yourself, while the forehead displays the words to others. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-11.html
- Matthew Henry: you can't expect good behaviour without good principles in the heart. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_011.cfm

**v. 19**
- Guzik, quoted on Precept Austin: you can measure your love for God's word by how much you talk about it with others. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62493/
- Matthew Henry: nothing does more for religion in a nation than bringing children up well. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_011.cfm

**v. 20**
- Barnes: the Jewish mezuzah is based on this verse and 6:9. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/6-9.html

**v. 21**
- Guzik, quoting Thompson: "as long as the heavens are above the earth" means "forever." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/
- Utley calls it a picture of permanence. https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-11
- Ellicott reports a Jewish comment: the text says the land was sworn to "give *them*" (the fathers, long dead), so the Law hints at the resurrection. He compares Acts 7:5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm

**v. 22**
- Guzik: "love, walk, hold fast" sum up all the commandments and describe a real relationship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/
- Ellicott cites Rashi on "walk in his ways": as God is compassionate, so you must be. He adds that what follows shows the need of a mediator. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm

**v. 23**
- Guzik: God fought for an obedient Israel (Joshua 10). Many people want God to fight for them but don't care to obey Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/

**v. 24**
- Guzik: the promise is repeated to Joshua (Joshua 1:3). Merrill notes that David and Solomon ruled all this, but the land east of the Jordan wasn't in the original promise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/

**v. 25**
- Guzik points to Joshua 2:9. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/
- Ellicott cites Rashi: "fear" for those nearby, "dread" for those far off. He sees it fulfilled across the Persian Empire in Esther. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm

**vv. 26–28**
- Guzik: the old covenant had three parts — law, sacrifice and choice. There was no neutral ground. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-11/
- Matthew Henry: blessing and curse are the law's rewards and punishments, appealing to hope and fear, those two handles of the soul. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_011.cfm
- Precept Austin: in v. 28, failing to "listen" is paired with "turning aside," so listening means obeying. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-11-commentary

**v. 29**
- Gill: the blessing and curse were spoken on, or facing, the two mountains. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/11-29.html
- Precept Austin: Joshua carried this out in Joshua 8:30–35. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-11-commentary
- Ellicott: the Targums speak of people turning to face each mountain as they blessed or cursed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm

**v. 30**
- Ellicott: the wording shows the speaker is east of the Jordan. Travellers have seen the sun set right in the gap between Ebal and Gerizim. "Plains of Moreh" should be "oaks of Moreh." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm
- NET note: the mountains are near ancient Shechem and modern Nablus. The valley between them works like an amphitheatre, and the place was sacred as the site of Abraham's first altar. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=Deu+11%3A28%2C29

**vv. 31–32**
- Ellicott: at the oak of Moreh God first promised this land to Abraham's descendants. Verse 32 ends the first part of the exposition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/11.htm
- Matthew Henry: obey, so that you don't become witnesses against yourselves at the coming ceremony. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_011.cfm

---

## 2. Where Christian readings differ

**vv. 26–28 (do the blessing and curse still apply to Christians?)**
- Guzik says no: we, in Jesus Christ, do not have an Old Covenant relationship with God. We expect to be blessed, not because of our obedience, but because of our position in Jesus. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Deu/Deu-11.cfm
- A Pulpit Commentary homily says the choice still turns on obedience: It was so under the Law, and it is so under the gospel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-11.html
- These two pull in different directions, but I couldn't find any denomination's own teachers addressing the question.

**v. 18 (literal or figurative?)**
- Hastings' dictionary lists Calvin, Jerome and Nicholas of Lyra (the latter two Catholic) among those who read the hand and forehead signs as figures of speech. It says most rabbis read them literally. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hdn/p/phylacteries.html
- GotQuestions takes them as figurative: what we do and think should be guided by God's word. https://www.gotquestions.org/phylacteries.html

---

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- **vv. 26–28:** The NET note says every surviving treaty from the late Bronze Age has a blessings-and-curses section. Here Moses previews chapters 27–28. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-11-commentary
- **vv. 10–12:** The Expositor's Bible assumes a later writer it calls "the Deuteronomist." It says he treats rain as a more direct sign of God's presence than the Nile's regular floods. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/deuteronomy/11.htm
- **vv. 18–20:** The 1901 Jewish Encyclopedia's "critical view" says the original wording was figurative, alluding to a common custom, and later rabbis read it literally. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/tje/p/phylacteries.html

**Jewish practice**
- **vv. 13–21:** This passage is one of the four placed inside tefillin, the scripture boxes Jewish men wear during prayer. https://www.gotquestions.org/phylacteries.html
